title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. title: What Price Settlement Speed? A Gabrielli–von Kármán Frontier for Financial Settlement Systems, from Babylonian Storehouses to Proof-of-Stake
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In 1950 Gabrielli and von Kármán asked "what price speed?" and answered with a single log-log chart: specific power plotted against velocity for every class of vehicle, bounded below by one limit line. This paper transposes that device to financial settlement. We define settlement velocity v = 1/τ as the inverse of the time to final settlement and specific exchange drag ε as the resource cost of settling one unit of value, in basis points, decomposed into four additive frictions: direct fees, risk and adverse-selection reserves, energy and hardware, and the opportunity cost of locked collateral. Placing six pre-industrial exemplars (c. 1750 BCE–1880) and fifteen modern systems on one diagram yields a nonparametric GvK Limit Line, the lower convex hull in log-log space, and a set of institutional regime envelopes. Two analytical results organise the diagram. First, the elasticity of drag with respect to the policy rate equals the collateral share of drag, which explains why netting shields systems from rate shocks. Second, when faster settlement destroys netting, transaction-window and balance-sheet accounting of collateral costs can disagree in sign; we call this the settlement liquidity paradox and apply it to the 2024 U.S. move to T+1.
